title: Given a set of distinct numbers, generate all possible permutations, meaning every possible ordering. Explain the backtracking technique that fixes one position at a time.
shortTitle: Permutations (Generate All Orderings of a Distinct Set)

s1_definition.oneliner: Fill positions one at a time, try each unused element, recurse, then undo the choice to explore all orderings.
s1_definition.profdef:
Permutations generates all n! orderings of n distinct elements using backtracking.

- **Choose** an unused element and add it to the current partial permutation.
- **Explore** by recursing to fill the next position with the remaining elements.
- **Unchoose** by removing the element and clearing its used flag so sibling branches start clean.
- **Base case** is reached when the current permutation holds all n elements, and a defensive copy is stored.
- **Used array** is a boolean array parallel to the input that tracks which elements are already placed.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a batch of three payments from Rajesh must be tried in every possible processing order to stress-test the settlement engine. We build an order one slot at a time: for the first slot we try each payment, for the next slot each remaining payment, and so on, undoing each choice to explore the next. When all slots are filled we have one complete ordering to test.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Permutations generates every ordering of a set of distinct elements, and there are n factorial of them. I use backtracking that fills the permutation one position at a time. I keep a current partial ordering and a boolean used array that marks which elements are already placed. At each level I loop over all elements, skip the used ones, and for each available element I choose it by adding it and marking it used, recurse to fill the next position, then unchoose by removing it and clearing the used flag so the next sibling choice can be explored.

The discipline I emphasize is choose, explore, unchoose, with the state restored exactly after every branch so sibling branches start clean. Because the elements are distinct, I do not need any duplicate skipping. If there were duplicates I would sort and skip equal siblings at the same level. I also state plainly that the number of permutations grows factorially, so this is only practical for small inputs.

At National Bank of India I used this to stress-test the settlement engine, which had to settle a batch of distinct payments correctly regardless of processing order, so we replayed every ordering of the batch through the engine. I generated the orderings with backtracking and a used array, storing each full ordering as a fresh copy.

The two alternatives worth knowing are the swap-based approach, which avoids the used array by swapping elements into position, and the next-permutation algorithm, which generates the lexicographic successor without storing all permutations.

Remember one sentence: fill positions one at a time with unused elements, recurse, then undo the choice to explore all n factorial orderings.

---

keyPoints: Permutations generates all n! orderings of n distinct elements using backtracking
The choose-explore-unchoose pattern marks an element used, recurses, then restores state
A boolean used array tracks which elements are already placed in the current permutation
A defensive copy must be stored when the permutation reaches full length
For duplicate elements, sort the input and skip equal siblings at the same recursion level
Factorial growth makes this feasible only for small n (n=10 produces 3.6 million permutations)
The swap-based alternative avoids the used array by swapping elements into position
